summary: Defines a CERT resource record so that public key certificates and certificate revocation lists can be stored in the DNS. It was replaced by RFC 4398.

eli5.summary: A digital ID card can be filed in the internet's phone book next to a name. This adds a new kind of entry for exactly that.

questions: what is a cert resource record
how to retrieve a certificate from dns
subtitle: A DNS resource record type for storing cryptographic certificates and revocation lists.

tldr.problem: Public key certificates are widely used to verify that a public key belongs to a specific entity, but they must be stored somewhere accessible. DNS is a logical place, but no standard way existed to store them there.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2538 defines a CERT resource record (type 37) for the Domain Name System that can hold X.509 certificates, PGP certificates, SPKI certificates, or other certificate types, each identified by a type code.
tldr.outcome: The CERT record allows certificates and certificate revocation lists to be retrieved via DNS queries, enabling applications to fetch certificate data from the domain name system.

today: RFC 2538 was obsoleted by RFC 4398, which updates the CERT record to support additional certificate types and provides refined guidance. The CERT resource record type 37 remains in use in DNS for storing certificates.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Public key certificates are widely used to verify that a public key truly belongs to a particular entity. A certificate is a digital document that cryptographically binds a public key to an identity, issued by a trusted signer. Certificate revocation lists (CRLs) are similarly signed documents that list certificates that have been revoked and are no longer valid.

This RFC defines a way to store these certificates and CRLs in the Domain Name System (DNS), the internet's distributed database of names and addresses. The CERT resource record (RR) allows a domain name to have associated certificate data, making it possible for applications to retrieve certificate information via standard DNS queries.
sections.eli5: A certificate is proof that a name on the internet is real, signed by someone trustworthy. This RFC lets you store that proof in DNS so anyone can look it up.

sections.title: The CERT Resource Record Format
sections.content:
The CERT resource record has type code 37 and contains four main fields. The type field identifies what kind of certificate is stored (X.509, PGP, SPKI, or others). The key tag is a 16-bit value computed from the key embedded in the certificate, used to quickly filter which CERT records might apply to a particular key without examining every certificate. The algorithm field indicates the cryptographic algorithm associated with the key, using the same values as DNS security records.

The fourth field holds the actual certificate or CRL data in binary form. When displayed as text in DNS zone files, this data is encoded in base64.
sections.eli5: A CERT record is like an envelope with labels that say what kind of certificate is inside, a quick reference number, which algorithm is used, and then the certificate itself.

sections.title: Certificate Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines several standard certificate types. Type 1 (PKIX) is for X.509 certificates conforming to the Internet Public Key Infrastructure profile. Type 2 is reserved for SPKI certificates (a format from an IETF working group). Type 3 is for PGP certificates as described in RFC 2440.

Types 4 through 252 are available for other uses. The RFC also reserves types 253 and 254 for private use: type 253 allows a certificate format to be specified by a URI, and type 254 allows it to be specified by an ISO OID (Object Identifier). This extensibility means new certificate types can be accommodated without changing the record format.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of certificates exist—ones from banks, from PGP, from other sources. The type field says which kind is in this envelope.

sections.title: Where to Store Certificates
sections.content:
The RFC recommends storing CERT records under domain names related to the certificate's subject (the entity that owns the private key) for regular certificates, and under names related to the certificate's issuer for revocation lists.

For X.509 certificates, the RFC gives guidance on priority. If the certificate contains a domain name, that domain should be used. If it contains an IP address, the reverse DNS name should be used. If it contains a URI with a domain name, that domain should be used. If it contains only a character string, that is handled similarly to PGP names. As a fallback, the certificate's distinguished name (DN) can be mapped to a domain name.
sections.eli5: A certificate usually has a name or email address in it. You file it in DNS under that same name, like filing alphabetically.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because certificates contain their own cryptographic signature, they are self-authenticating. It is safe to retrieve a certificate from non-secure DNS without verifying the DNS response, as long as the certificate's signature chain is verified back to a trusted root. The certificate itself, not the DNS answer, provides the security assurance.

Alternatively, if DNS security is enabled and verified, and a certificate is retrieved from a secure DNS zone with DNSSEC validation, the key within the certificate may be trusted without fully verifying the entire certificate chain, subject to the user's security policy.
sections.eli5: Certificates have their own signature, so the certificate itself proves it is real, not the DNS server. DNS security can add another layer of trust on top.

sections.title: Performance and Size Considerations
sections.content:
DNS was originally designed for small data transfers, typically under 512 bytes per response. Certificates can be large, especially certificate chains. The RFC recommends that certificates stored in DNS be kept as small as possible by using the minimum required fields and short values for variable-length fields.

Administrators should be mindful that large CERT records may require DNS responses larger than 512 bytes, which can trigger fallback to TCP or fragmentation, making lookups slower.
sections.eli5: DNS works best with small answers. Big certificates make DNS slower, so you should keep certificates compact when storing them.

fields.desc: 16-bit value computed from the key, for quick filtering.

fields.desc: The certificate or revocation list data, variable length.
